outcomes: Select and report a hardware Vulkan adapter without accepting a software fallback
Explain how Rust buffers and WGSL bindings represent the same contiguous [N] f32 vectors
Dispatch enough workgroups for an arbitrary element count without dropping the tail
Synchronize a real GPU result into a mapped readback buffer
Compare GPU output with the same scalar primitive using an explicit absolute-plus-relative tolerance
lessons: Why a GPU needs a different execution model
Discover the hardware you actually run
Move a vector through buffers and bindings
Dispatch WGSL and read the answer back
Run, debug, and extend the project

adapter.name: adapter
adapter.definition: A wgpu handle describing one available physical or software GPU implementation.
adapter.explanation: An adapter is the capability-discovery stage before a logical device is created. It reports a name, backend, device type, driver, limits, and optional features. A machine may expose several adapters, including an integrated GPU, a discrete GPU, or a CPU software implementation. Selecting one is part of experimental provenance: results only mean what you think they mean when the program prints which adapter and backend actually ran.

compute-shader.name: compute shader
compute-shader.definition: A GPU program launched over numbered invocations without drawing pixels.
compute-shader.explanation: A compute shader expresses one small operation that many GPU invocations execute. In this chapter the actual WGSL compute kernel is the add entry point, and each invocation adds one pair of vector elements. This use of kernel means GPU program; Chapter 16's statistical kernel K(a,b) is a similarity function with a different owning context. The Rust host still owns validation, buffer creation, binding, dispatch, and synchronization.

storage-buffer.name: storage buffer
storage-buffer.definition: A GPU-visible byte allocation exposed to a shader for indexed reads or writes.
storage-buffer.explanation: A storage buffer carries bulk values such as activations, weights, or outputs. The shader interprets its bytes according to a declared WGSL element type, while Rust uploads matching bytes. Usage flags are contracts: an input used by a shader needs STORAGE, a result copied out needs COPY_SRC, and a staging destination needs COPY_DST plus MAP_READ. Incorrect flags are validation errors rather than harmless hints.

workgroup.name: workgroup
workgroup.definition: A fixed-size group of shader invocations scheduled together and identified within a dispatch grid.
workgroup.explanation: The chapter uses workgroups of 64 invocations. Rust computes dispatch_count(element_count, workgroup_size) with ceiling division, so two workgroups launch 128 invocation IDs for 65 elements. The WGSL guard compares each ID with dispatch_params.element_count before indexing. Workgroup size is declared in WGSL, while workgroup count is chosen by Rust. Later chapters use the fact that invocations in one workgroup can share fast temporary memory and synchronize at barriers.

readback.name: readback
readback.definition: The synchronized copy and mapping that makes GPU-produced bytes visible to CPU code.
readback.explanation: GPU storage memory is not treated like an ordinary Rust slice. The program first copies output into a buffer created for MAP_READ, requests asynchronous mapping, and drives device progress until the callback completes. Only then may it view the bytes as f32 values. Mapping every intermediate result is costly and destroys device residency, so readback is best reserved for required outputs, diagnostics, or occasional metrics.

checks: The executable reports every discovered adapter and the selected hardware Vulkan adapter
A five-element vector is dispatched and read back from a real compute shader
Ordinary tests cover the scalar oracle, f32 tolerance, and exact and partial dispatch counts
The ignored hardware test covers 67 elements, including a partial workgroup
Empty, mismatched, and nonfinite inputs return errors before adapter discovery
limitations: The project creates a device for one operation rather than maintaining a long-lived compute context
The vector addition is a correctness demonstration, not a performance benchmark
Only the Vulkan backend is accepted for the course hardware path
GPU execution requires a hardware Vulkan adapter and fails explicitly when none is present
